scenes.narration: You open a map on your phone, and a blue dot settles on the street where you are standing. Nobody typed your address, so the phone worked the dot out from signals arriving on its own.

You already use this idea when a flash of lightning arrives before its thunder. Counting the seconds between them tells you how far away the strike was, because sound travels at a steady speed. That delay gives one distance, not a location.

Each GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal stamped with the time it was sent, plus information about its orbit. Your phone notes when that signal arrives, so travel time multiplied by the speed of light gives a range estimate.
That estimate is not yet exact, because the phone's own clock drifts a little. Until that clock error is accounted for, these distances are called pseudoranges.

This picture is a two-dimensional schematic. One range places you on a circle around its satellite. A second range, holding at the same time, leaves two possibilities where the circles cross. The real three-dimensional problem uses spheres instead, and must also solve the clock error.

Now count the unknowns: your three coordinates in space, plus the error in your phone's clock, which we call the clock offset. Four independent measurements from four satellites in suitable positions are solved together for all four at once, so your phone needs no atomic clock of its own. Real receivers often use more than four.

Take the speed of light as three hundred million metres per second. If a signal's time is off by one millionth of a second, multiply the two numbers, and the range error is about three hundred metres. That is a range error, not a guaranteed position error.

It is tempting to think three satellites pin you down and a fourth just measures altitude. That is not how it works, because your phone's clock error is unknown too, so the measurements are solved together, not one satellite per job.

So the blue dot comes from timing. A signal's travel time gives a range, several ranges narrow the possibilities, and four independent measurements from well-placed satellites are solved together for three coordinates and the clock offset. Real receivers often use more, and accuracy also depends on the atmosphere, reflected signals and satellite geometry.
